explanations.explanation: That's what the scribes say. Jesus opens with, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the Son of David?” (Mark 12:35). David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), and the scribes tie the Christ to his family. Hold on to that answer, friend, because Jesus is about to do something with it.

Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a giant in the Bible, so I get why he came to mind. But the text says the scribes call the Christ the Son of David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3). Right kind of big name, just a different family.

Aaron was Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), and he's a big name too. But the scribes in this passage say the Christ is the Son of David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3). I once spent years in a junk drawer and lost track of plenty of names, so I understand a mix-up. Mark 12:35 keeps it simple, though.

That's the one. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is speaking by the Holy Spirit, and the words are “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.” (Mark 12:36). A seat at the right hand, friend.

No packing needed on this one. Nothing in David's words sends anyone to Egypt. David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), speaks of the Lord telling his Lord to sit until the enemies are put under His feet (Mark 12:36). It's a seat, not a road trip.

Building a house does come up in David's own story, when God says David's offspring will build a house for His Name (2 Samuel 7:13). But that's not what's in the words Jesus quotes here. In Mark 12:36, the Lord's word to David's Lord is “Sit at My right hand…”
Not quite, friend. The text says “…the large crowd listened to Him with delight.” (Mark 12:37). Delight is a long way from upset.

You've got it. Mark 12:37 says “…the large crowd listened to Him with delight.” That's a big crowd, and they're happy to be there. If I had a crowd listening to me with delight, I'd probably need a lie down on my gold base.

That's right. The scribes want the chief seats in the synagogues and “…the places of honor at banquets.” (Mark 12:39). They want the best spot in the room. I spent years in a junk drawer, so I'd settle for any spot that isn't under a takeout menu.
Service is a good word, but it's not the one Jesus uses. The text says the scribes want “…the places of honor at banquets.” (Mark 12:39). Wanting honor is a different thing from wanting to serve.

Prayer does show up in this passage, just a verse later. Jesus says the scribes make lengthy prayers (Mark 12:40). But at banquets, the verse says they want “…the places of honor…” Same crowd of scribes, different spot in the sentence.

Yes, the word is show. Jesus says they “…for a show make lengthy prayers.” (Mark 12:40). Right before that, He says they defraud widows of their houses. Those words are heavy, and Jesus doesn't soften them.

Blessing is a lovely word, but it's not what Jesus says. In Mark 12:40, the scribes make lengthy prayers “…for a show…” The verse puts those prayers right next to defrauding widows of their houses. That's a heavy thing to read, friend.

Reward is close to the right track, but the verse uses a different word. Jesus says they “…for a show make lengthy prayers.” (Mark 12:40). The text doesn't tell us anything about a reward for the prayers. It just says show.
That's what Jesus says: “These men will receive greater condemnation.” (Mark 12:40). It comes right after He names what the scribes do. It's a serious line, so I'll leave it right there.

A double portion sounds like a gift, and it's not what this verse holds. Jesus says, “These men will receive greater condemnation.” (Mark 12:40). It's a heavy line, and the text gives us nothing about a double portion.

A long life would be a nice thing to hear about, but that's not it. Jesus says, “These men will receive greater condemnation.” (Mark 12:40). It's a heavy verse, and nothing in it mentions how long anyone lives.

That's what she brings. The text says one poor widow “…put in two small copper coins…” (Mark 12:42). That's all there is: two little coins. Keep your eye on them, friend, because Jesus is about to say something big about them.

A silver shekel would be a nice upgrade, but it's not what she brings. Mark 12:42 says she put in two small copper coins, which amounted to a small fraction of a denarius. Not a shekel in sight, friend.

Ten gold shekels would be a large amount, and the large amounts came from the rich people (Mark 12:41). This is a poor widow, and she puts in two small copper coins (Mark 12:42). If I had ten gold of anything, I'd have bought a bigger hat.

Yes, and Jesus says it plainly: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury.” That includes the many rich people who put in large amounts (Mark 12:41). He calls His disciples to Him to say it.

It's the other way, friend. Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury.” Not less than the rich people, more than all the others. It's a surprising line, and He says it to His disciples.

explanations.answer: She gave all she had to live on
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jesus gives. He says, “For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.” (Mark 12:44). The others gave from what was left over, and she gave everything she had to live on. Two coins, and Jesus says it's more than all of them.

The text doesn't say that. Jesus is sitting opposite the treasury, watching the crowd put money in (Mark 12:41). The reason He gives is in Mark 12:44: “…she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.” That's the point, friend.

explanations.answer: She gave before anyone else did
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says she went first. The verses say many rich people put in large amounts, and then one poor widow came (Mark 12:41-42). Jesus gives the reason in Mark 12:44: “For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.” It was never about who showed up first.
